sections.h2: Which office bills Albany property owners?
sections.html:
The Dougherty County Tax Department. One bill rolls together the county, City of Albany, school board and state levies, and the same office also takes vehicle, personal property, mobile home and timber accounts. Values come from the Board of Assessors, which is part of that department. The number on the county's bill notice is 229-431-3208.

Albany has no separate city bill to chase because it is Dougherty's only incorporated city as well as its seat. It stands on the Flint River in southwest Georgia, roughly 151 miles from Atlanta.

People confuse the two boards. One sets worth and hears value disputes, the assessors. The other, the commissioners, chooses the millage rate once the digest is final.

Georgia's default due date is December 20, but a county can set an earlier one or allow installments. The date printed on your own bill is the one that counts. Recent bill mailings have run late after state legislative changes, so read the date printed on the bill or call the Tax Department.

Albany property tax timing rules

Dougherty finished its first countywide revaluation in over a decade, and the 2026 notices carried fresh values. The notice is only a value statement. Taxes follow once appeals close, the digest is final and commissioners set the rate.

Two state laws shaped the notices. Senate Bill 566 changed the format, and the notice now shows:

  • the 45 day appeal deadline;
  • updated homestead exemption information;
  • estimated tax savings for qualifying owners.

Senate Bill 581 created the statewide floating homestead exemption, which can limit increases in the taxable value of a qualifying homestead.

Owners holding a qualifying 2026 homestead exemption also get the state's one-time Homeowner Tax Relief Grant, an $18,000 cut in assessed value, with no extra application. An inherited or vacant house without a homestead exemption misses it.

File in writing with the Board of Assessors inside the 45 day window. Georgia supplies a uniform form, and the grounds can include value, uniformity, taxability or a denied exemption.

That first filing also names the route: the Board of Equalization, a hearing officer or an arbitrator. The state revenue department cannot overrule these bodies on a single parcel. Bring any comparable sales, repair estimates and photographs you want considered. If you plan to sell soon, a lower value helps only for the tax year at issue, but it also gives you a cleaner record to show the buyer.

The statewide homestead exemption takes $2,000 off assessed value, and the tax is that reduced value times the millage rate. Assessed value runs 40 percent of market value. Apply by April 1 of the first year you want it, since skipping the application waives the exemption. Ask the Tax Department about any local additions.

The Board of Assessors also handles special assessments:

  • Preferential agricultural assessment, which values qualifying farm property at 30 percent of fair market value rather than 40 percent.
  • Conservation use assessment for certain agricultural, timber, environmentally sensitive and transitional residential land, valued at current use.
  • Forest land protection exemption for land used mainly for growing trees and timber.

Conservation applicants commit to ten years of qualifying use and may enroll at most 2,000 acres statewide. Anyone selling an enrolled tract should ask the Board of Assessors what the sale does to the commitment.

sections.h2: Taxes and transfer tax at closing
sections.html:
Whoever held title on January 1 owes the year's tax, and the state allows no refund to a partial year owner, so the contract and closing statement divide the bill.

The transfer tax runs $1 for the first $1,000 (or fraction) and 10 cents for each added $100 (or fraction) of price. The deed's signer is liable, though a contract may hand it to the buyer. Payment comes before recording at the Clerk of Superior Court, with the PT-61 declaration filed online through the state clerks' cooperative.

Closing steps in order: confirm the current bill is paid or prorated, order the transfer tax figure, file the PT-61, then record the deed. A cash buyer can move through these quickly, but none of them is skipped.

An open bill is easiest to handle before the sign goes up. Phone the Tax Department at 229-431-3208 for the exact balance and ask whether interest is accruing. The January 1 owner is on the hook for the full year, so buyers usually expect you to pay or prorate it, and an unpaid amount is simply held out of your proceeds at the table.

Request a written payoff, hand it to the closing attorney, and keep your receipt. A cash buyer can shorten the timeline, but the payoff letter and transfer tax figure still have to be ready before the deed is recorded.

A home near the Flint River raises a flood question. The river damaged property in 1841 and 1925, Tropical Storm Alberto brought a severe flood in 1994, and the river crested at 35 feet above its bed in 1998. The city decided against redeveloping parts of its riverfront floodplain. Ask city staff about floodplain status for a given address.

In January 2017 an EF3 tornado hit the south side, and in October 2018 Hurricane Michael tracked through south Georgia. If your house had storm repairs, keep the damage history, permits and receipts together for the buyer.

The tax paperwork has three parts: the Tax Department's bill for the parcel, the Board of Assessors' value and exemption record, and the transfer tax certification the Clerk of Superior Court attaches to the deed. Ask for each early, so nothing delays the closing date.

If taxes are still owed, call 229-431-3208 for a payoff and have the title company confirm it. If you hold a farm or timber enrollment, bring that file to the Board of Assessors before you list.

sections.h2: Utilities and services a buyer will ask about
sections.html:
Albany Water, Gas & Light, a municipal commission, supplies water, gas and electricity to its customers, although parts of Albany are served by Georgia Power. The public water supply comes from four aquifers. The city reports a fire protection rating of ISO 2, and the county landfill on Gaissert Road handles solid waste. Albany Transit System buses connect the city and the county.

Public safety splits by territory. The Albany Fire Department operates 11 stations in Dougherty County, seven of them inside the city limits, and the Albany Police Department is organized into three districts. The Dougherty County Police Department covers the unincorporated area. The city also has a tree ordinance and a certified arborist on staff, so ask the city before removing a large tree.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a delinquent Albany property tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Dougherty County Tax Department at 229-431-3208. One bill covers all four levies.

faqs.q: Is there a separate City of Albany bill?
faqs.a: No. The county department folds city tax into the same bill as county, school and state tax.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to dispute an Albany value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the mailing of the assessment notice, filed in writing with the assessors.

faqs.q: Does the $18,000 grant reach a rental in Albany?
faqs.a: It goes only to homesteads with a qualifying 2026 exemption, which rules out rentals and vacant houses.

faqs.q: Who owes transfer tax on an Albany sale?
faqs.a: State law makes the seller liable, and the contract may reassign it.
